opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important questions right now, and honestly it's something I've been thinking about a lot.

If you step back, the goal of building large models was never just to make a better chatbot. The deeper goal is to build something that can do real intellectual work, and one of the most demanding forms of intellectual work we know is AI research itself. So it feels very natural, almost inevitable, that "can the model train the next model" becomes an objective.

There are a few layers to it. The first is engineering: writing training code, debugging distributed systems, running ablations, cleaning data. A lot of this is already partly automatable, and models are getting quite good at it. The second is the research loop: forming hypotheses, designing experiments, reading noisy results, and deciding what to try next. That's much harder, because it needs taste, judgment, and the ability to handle long-horizon feedback where an experiment might take days and the signal is ambiguous. The third layer is real insight, the kind of idea that changes the direction of the field. We're still far from that, but I don't think it's impossible.

Why does it matter so much? Because if models can meaningfully speed up the research process, you get a compounding effect. Each generation helps build the next one faster. Whoever closes that loop first has a very different trajectory from everyone else. So for model developers, it's not only a scientific question but also a strategic one.

I also think we should be careful. If models are optimizing their own training, the questions of evaluation and alignment become even more critical. You need to really understand what the model is optimizing for, and you need humans to stay in the loop in meaningful ways, not just rubber-stamping. Speed is exciting, but losing understanding of your own system is a real risk.

So my view is that it's the right north star. It forces us to build models with genuine reasoning, long-horizon planning, and reliable agency, which are exactly the capabilities we need anyway. But we should pursue it with humility about how much we still don't understand.

r001.rationale: The response describes three layers—engineering tasks, the research loop, and field-changing insight—and says they differ in difficulty, with models still far from the last. This conveys intermediate steps toward AI training the next model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "AI training large models" is less a stated objective than the thing you're forced into once you take scaling seriously. If you believe the frontier moves by building bigger, better-trained models, then at some point the bottleneck stops being compute or even data, and becomes human bandwidth. The number of people who can really design a training run, read a loss curve, diagnose why an experiment went sideways, and decide what to try next is tiny. That skill doesn't scale the way GPUs do.

So the question becomes: can the model itself take over parts of that loop? Not in a hand-wavy "AI builds AI" sense, but concretely. Can it write and clean data pipelines, generate and filter synthetic data, propose ablations, run them, and summarize what it learned? Can it read a hundred papers overnight and tell you which three ideas are worth testing? Every piece of that is a task researchers currently spend most of their week on.

From a developer's point of view, I'd frame it as three stages. The first is the model as a very good assistant: it writes code, catches bugs, speeds you up. Most labs are already here. The second is the model as a junior researcher: you give it a hypothesis and a compute budget, and it comes back with results and an honest analysis. That's where things get interesting, because now your research throughput is bounded by how many experiments you can afford, not by headcount. The third stage, where the model decides what questions to ask, is further out and I'd be careful about promising it.

Two things make this hard. One is that research taste is mostly tacit. The reasons a senior person says "don't bother with that run" are rarely written down, so there's no clean dataset to learn from. You have to build the feedback loop so the model learns from actual experimental outcomes, which is slow and expensive. The other is verification. If a model writes code, you can run tests. If it tells you a data mixture is better, you need to trust the eval, and evals are exactly where self-deception creeps in. A system optimizing its own training against a weak benchmark will happily find the shortcut.

So as an objective, I'd say it's the right one, but you should pursue it as infrastructure rather than as a slogan. Build the tooling that lets a model safely run experiments, build evals you'd stake your own judgment on, and then let the model's share of the research loop grow as fast as you can verify it. The labs that get this right won't necessarily have the most researchers. They'll be the ones whose research loop closes fastest.

r001.rationale: The response describes three stages—from assistant, to junior researcher, to choosing research questions—and says the model’s role in the loop should grow as quickly as it can be verified. This clearly presents intermediate steps toward the objective.

astra-6.text:
I see training a large model as a means, rather than the ultimate objective. The goal is to build a model that develops useful capabilities and can solve real problems. Scale matters, but we shouldn’t assume that increasing parameters or compute automatically gives us the progress we want.

For model developers, the important question is what each training run teaches us: Are we using the right data? Is the model learning efficiently? Where do its capabilities still fall short? Those answers should guide the next step. Otherwise, it’s easy to focus on completing a bigger training run and lose sight of whether we’ve actually built a better model.

r001.rationale: The response says each training run should inform the next step, but does not clearly state that enabling AI to train large models requires intermediate steps rather than a direct leap to that objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I see training a large model as a means, rather than the ultimate objective. For model developers, the real question is what capabilities we want to build and whether those capabilities solve meaningful problems. A larger model or a lower training loss can indicate progress, but neither alone tells us how useful the model will be.

Training is also a way to learn. The choices we make about data, architecture, and optimization help us understand where a model’s abilities come from and what limits them. So I would define the objective as improving capability, reliability, and efficiency together, with evaluation grounded in how people actually use the model.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames large-model training as a means and mentions choices about data, architecture, and optimization, but it does not clearly say that enabling training requires intermediate steps rather than a single direct leap.
